fact_sheet.business_description: The Coca-Cola Company sells branded beverage concentrates through a worldwide bottling and distribution system [D01]. The company focuses on its beverage franchise, leveraging recognized brand names to generate repeat consumer demand [D01].
products_customers_and_why_they_buy: Concentrates for soft drinks sold through bottling and distribution networks [D01].
Repeat consumer demand and brand recognition serve as primary drivers of sales [D01].
economics: Concentrate model separates brand and concentrate returns from bottler capital requirements [D02].
Return on average equity from continuing operations was 27.2% in 1987; 28.8% in 1986 [D02].
Requires advertising, product quality, and route-to-market access [D01].
competitive_position: Global soft-drink share of more than 44% (excluding Soviet Union/China) [D06].
Fountain business outsold nearest rival by more than two to one [D06].
Distribution reach of more than 155 countries [D06].
management_and_capital_allocation: Roberto Goizueta (CEO) and Don Keough have emphasized the beverage franchise and financial discipline since 1981 [D01].
Focus on expansion of the beverage business abroad [D03].

yields_pct.basis: Trailing earnings yield and dividend yield are based on Dec 31, 1987 data [D04]. Long bond yield is as of Sept 30, 1988 [D04].

what_the_market_is_worried_about: Dilution from capital-heavy bottling investments and unrelated activities [D05].
berkshire_context: Existing major interests include Capital Cities/ABC, GEICO, and Washington Post [D08].
Exact September 1988 liquidity and beverage allocation not in pack [D08].
document_conflicts: 1986 return on equity: 28.8% reported in [D02], cited as 23.8% in secondary transcription [D02].

understandable.evidence: The company maintains a dominant, global beverage franchise with products that face slow-changing consumer preferences [D01].

durable_moat_and_pricing_power.evidence: Coca-Cola possesses massive brand recognition and a global distribution network with a 44% market share [D06].

consistent_earnings_record.evidence: Net income has shown consistent growth from $559 million in 1983 to $916 million in 1987 [D02].

high_roe_little_debt.evidence: Return on average equity reached 27.2% in 1987, and the company maintains a manageable net debt position [D02].

capital_intensity.evidence: The concentrate model successfully separates the high-return brand business from the capital-intensive bottling operations [D02].

able_honest_owner_minded_management.evidence: Management has demonstrated disciplined focus on the core beverage franchise and international expansion since 1981 [D01], [D03].

size_moves_the_needle.evidence: The company's scale is substantial enough to meaningfully impact Berkshire's portfolio [D06], [D08].

price_screen.evidence: The earnings yield of 6.37% [D04] is well below the 10%+ requirement relative to the 8.87% long bond yield [D04].

conflicts_resolved: 1986 ROE → used 28.8% from primary source [D02] as it is consistent with the reported multi-year profitability trend.
gate1.one_line_business_quality_verdict: a world-class consumer franchise with a powerful moat and excellent returns on capital, currently priced too high to meet our margin of safety

gate2.why_available: There is no reason to expect a bargain at current market levels. While Coca-Cola is a wonderful business, the market is currently reflecting its quality and growth potential in a premium valuation that leaves no margin of safety [D04], [D05].
evidence: Earnings yield of 6.37% is well below the required 10% threshold [D04].
Long bond yield of 8.87% exceeds the earnings yield, offering little premium for equity risk [D04].
gate2.market_narrative_we_disagree_with: The market believes the brand is fully valued at current prices and is concerned about potential dilution from bottling investments or currency headwinds [D05].
what_must_be_true: The business continues to compound earnings at high rates to justify the premium valuation.
The company maintains its dominant global market share and pricing power.
Management continues to focus on the core beverage franchise over unrelated diversification.

gate3.owner_earnings_per_share: 1.80 (Assumed normalized EPS of 2.43 [D02] less 0.63 maintenance capex per share [Assumption based on 1987 capital intensity])
gate3.price_vs_value: Price exceeds low-end intrinsic value; no margin of safety.
gate3.alternatives: Long bonds at 8.87% [D04] offer a superior risk-adjusted return compared to an equity yielding 4.72% pretax.
gate3.downside_case: Multiple compression due to market re-rating of the premium franchise; loss is unlikely to be permanent if business quality endures, but valuation risk is significant.
flagged_assumptions: Maintenance capex estimated at 0.63 per share to calculate owner earnings as data is not in pack.
September 30, 1988 price not in pack; valuation based on 1987 year-end price of 38.13 [D04].

gate4.role_description: We are a permanent, passive holder of marketable securities. We look for wonderful businesses at fair prices and hold them indefinitely, relying on the company's compounding power and rational capital allocation to build value over time [D01].
value_realisation_path: Value is realised through the underlying business's ability to compound owner earnings at high rates of return [D02].
gate4.why_this_role_fits_the_era: In the 1980-1999 era, our primary focus is on identifying durable consumer franchises with pricing power and management that acts like owners, holding these through our permanent capital base rather than attempting to control or restructure them [D01], [D03].

kill_criteria: Permanent loss of pricing power to private label competitors
Management acquires assets significantly outside the core beverage franchise
International markets fail to sustain growth trajectory
Return on equity collapses due to unsuccessful heavy capital investment in bottling
gate5.berkshire_constraints: Must maintain adequate liquidity for insurance operations and future acquisition opportunities; capital allocation must avoid tax-inefficient churning [D01], [D08].
gate5.opportunity_cost: Capital is better deployed into long-term Treasury bonds yielding 8.87% [D04] or held for businesses meeting our 10% earnings yield threshold [D01].
gate5.decider_reason: Buffett directly manages the equity portfolio and major capital allocation decisions.
gate5.biggest_risk_in_one_sentence: Paying a premium price that offers no margin of safety relative to prevailing long-term interest rates.

valuation.downside_case: Significant multiple compression due to current premium valuation.

drivers.driver: The company's earnings yield of 6.37% is well below our 10% threshold and significantly trails the 8.87% long-term Treasury bond yield [D04].
Coca-Cola is a wonderful business, but the market currently prices it for perfection, leaving no margin of safety for an investor [D04], [D05].
The business operates a global beverage franchise with a 44% market share and consistently high returns on equity, exceeding 27% [D02], [D06].
The concentrate model allows the company to generate superior economics by separating brand-building from the capital-intensive bottling system [D02].
Management, led by Roberto Goizueta, has remained disciplined, focusing on core beverage expansion and consistent financial returns since 1981 [D01], [D03].

kill_criteria: Permanent loss of pricing power to private label competitors
Management acquires assets significantly outside the core beverage franchise
International markets fail to sustain growth trajectory
Return on equity collapses due to unsuccessful heavy capital investment in bottling
final.what_would_change_our_mind: A significant decline in the stock price that would offer an initial pre-tax earnings yield of at least 10% relative to the long bond yield, or a fundamental change in the business's ability to compound earnings.
final.memo:
The Coca-Cola Company is a quintessential consumer franchise, possessing a powerful global brand and a distribution network that reaches over 155 countries [D06]. We understand this business well, as it sells simple beverage concentrates that create repeat consumer demand through a model that is remarkably capital-light at the brand level [D01], [D02].

Its record of performance is exceptional, with net income growing from $559 million in 1983 to $916 million by 1987 [D02]. The company maintains a durable moat, evidenced by a 44% global soft-drink share and return on equity levels that have reached as high as 28.8% [D02], [D06].

Roberto Goizueta and Don Keough have proven to be able, owner-minded managers who have consistently prioritized the core beverage franchise and international expansion over unrelated diversification [D01], [D03]. They act with a level of discipline that we admire, ensuring that the company's capital allocation serves the long-term health of the brand [D01].

Despite these sterling qualities, the market has left us no room to purchase the business at a bargain price. With the long bond yielding 8.87%, an equity yielding only 6.37% offers no margin of safety for the risks inherent in the stock market [D04]. Even for a wonderful business, the price must be right; at current levels, the market has fully priced in future success [D04], [D05].

While we believe the business will continue to thrive, we are not willing to pay a premium that offers a lower yield than a risk-free government bond [D04]. We prefer to wait for Mr. Market to offer us a more sensible entry point, as we have no need to force activity when better risk-adjusted returns are available elsewhere [D01].
